item.title: Windows 11 has a “feature” that throttles performance, but disabling it has a security tradeoff
item.itunes:title: Windows 11 has a “feature” that throttles performance, but disabling it has a security tradeoff
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
It's rare that a security vulnerability affects a huge swath of processors all at once, but the Spectre vulnerabilities that were uncovered in 2018 were so widespread that they forced operating system vendors to trade performance for protection. Windows started carrying mitigations to protect against it that were on by default, and it did take sacrificing some CPU performance. They're still enabled by default today, and users can switch it off if they please with a simple registry tweak. Whether doing so is a smart optimization measure or just an unnecessary risk depends on what the machine is used for and the age of the CPU, and the latter matters a lot more than it used to.

This one Windows 11 update made my PC faster and consume less RAM, and I didn't change a single setting

There's no reason not to upgrade to 26H2

By  Abhinav Raj

The Spectre mitigations are still active

A family of attack vectors on speculative execution

Spectre is a family of different attacks on the same processor technique called speculative execution, which is used in virtually every modern CPU. Processors use this technique to stay fast by guessing ahead as to where the code will go, and discarding the incorrect guesses. Traces of those incorrect guesses linger in the cache, and with a carefully written program, someone could feasibly infer sensitive data based on those traces. The variant that takes advantage of that mechansim is the Spectre variant 2, or branch target injection, where an attacker trains the CPU's branch predictor to steer the speculation somewhere useful for them, such as into the kernel code that handles secrets.

The mitigations that Windows put in place restricts that kind of speculation that happens at the boundary between apps and the kernel, and that's where the performance cost lies. It's not a throttle as much as it is just a bit of extra work that happens every time a program hands something off to the OS. Workloads that cross a lot of boundaries of the system often, like storage and code compiling, feel this a lot more. Anything that runs solely on the CPU cores themselves and doesn't call into the kernel won't really notice a performance impact.

7 apps that could be slowing your Windows performance

Is your Windows laptop feeling sluggish? These seven apps could be affecting performance.

6
By  Saeed Wazir

The performance cost can be real

Microsoft admitted that it can have a significant impact

When Microsoft shipped these mitigations in 2018, it released them along with their own testing, which showed single-digit slowdowns on WIndows 10 PCs with Skylake or newer Intel processors. On Haswell and older, some benchmarks showed larger drops that users would definitely feel a bit more. Microsoft also noted that the first Spectre variant and Meltdown could be patched without significant slowdowns, which left variant 2 as the expensive one to patch as far as performance went.

The registry value FeatureSettingsOverride controls which OS-side mitigations are turned on, and there are some free utilities out there that you can use to turn these off without regedit along with others, such as the mitigations for Meltdown. If you were to change the registry value to the value most commonly shared online, 3, you would disable Meltdown protection as well, while a value of 1 turns off only the Spectre variant 2 mitigation. Either way, the change affects only the operating system’s side of the defense.

I make this one change to make Windows faster

One simple toggle can speed up your Windows experience

15
By  Ty Sherback

Newer CPUs don't benefit as much

The newer you get, the less you gain from turning off Spectre mitigations

  • Credit: htomari | Flickr
  • Credit: Wikimedia Commons
  • Credit: htomari | Flickr
  • Credit: Wikimedia Commons

Newer chips fix some of these flaws directly in silicon and make the rest cheaper to mitigate, and Windows itself moved to lower-overhead mitigation techniques like retpoline back in 2019. On a recent Ryzen or Intel processor, disabling the mitigation in the OS probably won’t give you any measurable performance increase. The risk of doing so also isn't purely theoretical, either. In 2021, researcher Julien Voisin found working Spectre exploits for Windows and Linux uploaded to VirusTotal. They were traced back to Immunity’s commercial penetration-testing platform, Canvas. Later, in 2024, researchers at Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam demonstrated an attack called Native BHI that leaked kernel memory on Intel systems running Linux despite the protections already being in place, and Microsoft has continued publishing guidance for newer variants.

Of course, for these types of exploits, malicious code has to exist and be actively running on the machine, so something that exclusively plays games or lives in the living room as a media box isn't really at risk for these types of exploits. Turning off Spectre might not net you a terrible amount of performance, but Microsoft does point to Memory Integrity and the Virtual Machine Platform as features that can hurt performance in specific scenarios, though turning those off comes with their own set of potential security trade-offs.

I make this one change to make Windows faster

One simple toggle can speed up your Windows experience

15
By  Ty Sherback

Spectre mitigations are there for a reason

While disabling Spectre mitigations to increase performance isn't a complete myth, they're not nearly as effective as the used to be. On a decade-old processor, it can return real performance to workloads that lean on the kernel and cross between different components on the system, but on a modern CPU, it trades away protection for a few benchmark points. Whether that's worth it for you will come down to your specific system and workload.

item.title: I explored 5 code editors beyond VS Code, and one was clearly ahead
item.itunes:title: I explored 5 code editors beyond VS Code, and one was clearly ahead
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
VS Code has become my go-to recommendation for coding, but I started wondering what I might be missing by sticking with the same editor. There are plenty of alternatives out there, each with its own approach to writing and managing code. So, I decided to explore five options that caught my attention, from traditional text editors to AI-powered coding environments. I wanted to see what made each one worth considering, where they fell short, and whether any could offer a better everyday experience. One of them surprised me more than I expected.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Kate

A simple text editor that does more than I expected

Kate felt like a practical option when I wanted an editor that stayed out of my way. It comes with a clean interface, syntax highlighting for multiple programming languages, and useful features that make working with code easier. I particularly liked its split-view editing, which let me work with two files side by side without constantly switching between tabs.

Kate also includes a built-in terminal, making it convenient to run commands without leaving the editor. Its session support helps me pick up where I left off, while the search and replace tools make navigating larger files less tedious. However, Kate feels more like a traditional text editor than a modern development environment. It's a solid choice for everyday editing, but I wanted something more ambitious.

Devin Desktop

A different approach to getting coding work done

Devin Desktop caught my attention because it takes a different approach to working with code. Rather than focusing only on editing files, it brings Devin's AI software engineering capabilities into a desktop environment. I could use it to delegate coding tasks, work through project requirements, and let an AI agent handle parts of the implementation.

What interested me most was the idea of moving beyond asking for code suggestions and giving an agent a more complete task to work on. This approach could be useful when I need to explore an unfamiliar codebase or tackle repetitive development work. However, I still needed to review the output carefully and make sure the changes matched my requirements.

Devin Desktop felt more like a workspace for AI-assisted development than a conventional code editor. That distinction made it interesting, although it wasn't quite the traditional editing experience I was looking for.

Cursor

AI features that fit naturally into my coding workflow

The familiar interface made it easy for me to get started without spending much time learning a new layout. What stood out was how easily I could ask questions about my code, generate changes, and work with multiple files using natural-language instructions.

I found its codebase awareness particularly useful. Instead of explaining every file and function manually, I could ask it to help me understand how different parts of a project worked together. Its inline editing also made it convenient to refine existing code without interrupting my workflow.

However, AI is central to the experience, and getting the most out of it means relying on AI throughout development. I liked the convenience, but I wanted to see whether another editor could offer a better overall balance of performance, simplicity, and everyday usability.

I compared VS Code, Cursor, and Google Antigravity for 30 days, and one pulled far ahead

One tool simply felt ahead.

15
By  Parth Shah

Nevoim

A keyboard-driven editor that rewards patience

I had to adjust my usual editing habits to get comfortable with Neovim. It uses a keyboard-focused, modal editing system, so I could navigate files, select text, and make changes without constantly reaching for the mouse. Once I started getting used to its commands, even routine editing tasks felt more efficient.

What impressed me was how much control it offered. I could customize the editor with Lua, add plugins for my preferred workflow, and use its built-in language server support for features such as code navigation and diagnostics. Its terminal integration was another useful addition, keeping common development tasks close at hand.

The downside was the learning curve. Neovim requires more setup and patience than most graphical editors. I appreciated its flexibility, but I wanted an editor that felt powerful without demanding so much configuration.

Zed

The editor that got the balance right

What stood out to me about Zed was its focus on performance. Built with Rust, it is designed to keep editing responsive without the overhead of an Electron-based editor. Moving between files, navigating projects, and working with multiple panes felt smooth. I also liked how the clean interface kept the focus on my code instead of surrounding it with too many panels and menus.

Zed offers several useful features without requiring me to build my entire workflow around extensions. Its built-in Git integration lets me review changes, inspect diffs, and manage my work directly in the editor. Language server support adds familiar development features such as code completion, diagnostics, and navigation, while the integrated terminal lets me run commands without switching applications.

I was also interested in its approach to AI and collaboration. Zed supports AI-assisted coding, including inline edits and chat, with options to connect different model providers. Its real-time collaboration features let developers work together in a shared editing environment.

After a month with VS Code, Cursor, and Zed, I finally found the editor that gets out of the way

I spent a month switching editors, and one finally made me stop looking.

3
By  Yash Patel

The editor that earned a place in my workflow

Exploring these five editors reminded me that the most popular tool isn't always the right fit for everyone. Each one has something different to offer, but Zed stood out as the editor I wanted to spend more time with. It balances a focused interface with useful features without making the experience feel complicated. VS Code remains a solid choice, but if you're curious about trying something new, Zed deserves a spot on your shortlist.

Zed

Zed is an open-source, high-performance code editor and modular development environment (IDE) designed for Windows, macOS, and Linux.

item.title: Nintendo Switch games can now run on Mac thanks to a Wine-like tool, and 85 titles are already compatible
item.itunes:title: Nintendo Switch games can now run on Mac thanks to a Wine-like tool, and 85 titles are already compatible
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Nxnative runs Switch ARM64 code on iPhone/iPad/Mac, rebuilding Switch graphics on Metal.
  • About 85 Switch titles are already compatible with Nxnative, including Mario Kart 8, Super Mario Odyssey, and Tears of the Kingdom.
  • You need to build each IPA or .app via the command line, Xcode 27.1, and Homebrew.

We've already seen a few Switch games make their way to Mac unofficially, notably The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom. Several of these early projects are tied to MacNativeGames, a tool that runs the game's original ARM64 code directly on Apple hardware and rewrites instructions as needed for macOS, iOS, and iPadOS compatibility, which is built on parts of dr2-mobile.

Nxnative's key advantage over similar apps is that it turns a technique previously demonstrated for individual games into a broader shared framework that can be applied to other titles. Roughly 85 Switch games are already compatible with the tool, including Mario Kart 8 Deluxe, Super Mario Odyssey, The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom, Dragon Quest XI S: Echoes of an Elusive Age, and several more.

There's even a community-made Mac app called NX2Apple with a GUI that streamlines the process, though seedds, Nxnative's creator, describes it as a "separate project that follows this one." Otherwise, you'll need to use the command line, Xcode 27.1, and Homebrew to build the unsigned IPA or .app for each title. With Nxnative, some Switch games support higher frame rates than on the handheld, plus render scaling and more. Most games seem to run at the same frame rates as on the regular Switch, which vary widely by title.

"Nothing from any game is in this repository, and the project is not affiliated with Nintendo or any game publisher," writes seedds on the project's GitHub repository. This means that, like similar port projects, you'll need to dump your own Switch games to use Nxnative.

Someone just got the Switch 2's Mario Kart World running on a Mac, and Nintendo probably isn't thrilled

The game is still a bit of a mess, but it seems playable.

By  Patrick O'Rourke

It's a new era for Switch ports on Mac

Nxnative runs Switch code directly on Mac, iPhone, and iPad

I haven't tried Nxnative myself yet, but based on a video from YouTuber Andrew Tsai (check it out above), most supported games seem to run reasonably well, though some titles have graphics and performance issues. Because Nintendo's Switch and Apple's modern iPhones, iPads, and Macs use Arm-based processors, Nxnative can run much of a Switch game's original code directly on Apple hardware.

It also recreates the Horizon OS services that Switch games depend on, including thread scheduling, synchronization, filesystem access, and memory management. The tool also lowers the overall hardware overhead required to play Switch games smoothly, giving it a key advantage over more traditional Mac Switch emulators like Astris.

In fact, like Wine, nxnative acts as a compatibility layer, allowing software written for another platform to execute on the host operating system. It uses high-level emulation (HLE) to recreate Horizon system services, while translating Switch graphics operations into Metal. Nxnative also uses work from several other projects, including Ryujinx for its shader translator and Yuzu for its "Maxwell instruction encodings for the shader reference tool, and a cross-check for kernel behavior."

In other port-related news, a fork of Nxnative recently got Switch 2 title Mario Kart World running on a Mac. This is the first time a Switch 2 game has run successfully on another device.

With files from Adam Conway.

For once, Mac gets a game first as Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom now runs natively on Apple's M4 chip

Nintendo likely isn't happy about this very unofficial port.

By  Patrick O'Rourke

item.title: I regret connecting these 4 devices to smart plugs, and I wish someone told me sooner
item.itunes:title: I regret connecting these 4 devices to smart plugs, and I wish someone told me sooner
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Smart plugs are great. They let you remotely power devices on and off when these controls are not available natively. For this reason, I have connected several devices to smart plugs over the last year. And for the most part, they proved to be a valuable addition to my home. But there were a couple of instances that made me realize that smart plugs are not the perfect choice for every device.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

They do work great with simple devices and appliances like lamps and coffee makers. I even use my smart plugs to charge a couple of old speakers I have lying around. I usually plug them in before I go to bed and set the smart plug to cut off power after a couple of hours. And it has worked well so far. On the other hand, there were times when I regretted connecting a device to a smart plug, mostly because of the associated risks. On a handful of occasions, though, the smart plugs simply proved counterproductive, creating the same problems they were intended to solve.

Smart TVs

Especially the OLED models

TVs are among the first things I would take off smart plugs, particularly OLED models. Honestly, I had both my TVs connected to smart plugs, and I quickly realized they were not a great choice for several reasons. First, a smart plug can't really turn the TV back on. You will still need the remote for it. All it helps with is setting a time limit.

More importantly, a smart plug can damage your TV, both on the hardware and software level. If you have an OLED TV, it's worth knowing that it runs a critical maintenance routine in standby mode. Called Pixel Refresh, it detects any wear individual pixels have undergone over time and applies the necessary corrections to maintain image quality. The same thing happens with your OLED monitor. And your smart plug can potentially harm it by powering off the TV while the routine is underway. Apart from that, if the smart plug accidentally shuts off and resumes power in quick succession, the sudden surge can damage your TV. Similarly, the smart plug can cut power during updates, which can also cause issues.

This may not apply to every model, but the risks are worth considering. Personally, I no longer have the main TV connected to the smart plug. It's directly plugged into the wall socket. The older TV model still uses a smart plug. That's because it has survived years of rough handling, and whatnot, and I don't think a smart plug will do much harm at this point.

Your smart TV is the worst-behaved device on your network, and taming it needs a simple fix

You need to optimize your Wi-Fi to accommodate your older smart TV

By  Tanveer Singh

Rooms heaters

Anything dangerous should never be on smart plugs

Another device you should never connect to smart plugs is a heater, even a compact one. Frankly, it's not just heaters, but anything that generates heat or is even remotely dangerous. I am not getting into the power surge or durability arguments here because those are secondary. The primary concern is safety.

I agree. Smart plugs are generally reliable, but there are instances when they don't respond to remote controls. I have had my fair share of problems. It could be a temporary glitch or a connectivity issue to blame. When that happens, you can't power off the heater, which is a major safety risk. Devices like these should always be operated under supervision, and while I am not entirely against occasional automation, you are better off connecting them directly to the wall outlet or getting one that natively supports remote control.

I let Home Assistant run my heating for a whole winter, and these are the automations that actually saved money

I didn't have to put on more clothes either.

By  Rich Edmonds

Refrigerators and washing machines

Avoid high-power appliances

These two do seem like an exciting application for smart plugs, especially if you have an older model that doesn't offer remote management or automation, but believe me, you couldn't be more wrong. In the past year, only one of my smart plugs failed entirely, and it was the one I connected to my washer.

The problem with these appliances is that they don't always draw a constant current. Instead, the current fluctuates and can sometimes spike to 2-3x the rated amperage, which may exceed what your smart plug can handle. And this directly affects the smart plug's lifespan. At least, that's what I guess happened to mine. Again, using them occasionally may not pose as much harm, but prolonged exposure most certainly will.

I replaced my smart bulbs with smart relays and saved my family from home automation fatigue

Your smart home shouldn't cause friction.

42
By  Jasmine Mannan

Home router

Learned my lesson the hard way

As surprising as it may sound, this was one of the smart plug uses I advocated for the longest. The idea is simple: you connect your router to a smart plug and configure it to automatically reboot the router once a month or so, at a time when no one is likely to be using the internet. Those periodic reboots helped improve overall network stability, but automating it with a smart plug wasn't the right choice, as I soon found out.

Despite being generally reliable, smart plugs are prone to the occasional glitches. This means they can turn off your router at the worst possible times. Mine would automatically turn off during meetings and critical uploads, and it happened with every smart plug I tried—more often on some than others. I am not saying it will happen every day, but even once a month is enough to ditch the idea. And that's what I did.

Those occasional reboots still happen, but instead of the smart plug, I walk up to the router, unplug it, wait for a minute, and then power it back on.

Stop using Wi-Fi for your smart home

You're crippling your own internet speeds

25

item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
My Home Assistant setup is the backbone of my smart home. However, it's not a setup that I've built overnight. It's taken me years to settle on what I have today. From a Raspberry Pi to my current NAS-based setup, I did a lot of trial and error getting the right hardware in place and everything set up. Enough that I wished that there was a more appliance-like approach to the problem. Yes, I'm aware that Home Assistant Green exists, but if I'm using a piece of hardware as the central part of my smart home ecosystem, it should be able to do more.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

That's how I came across the SwitchBot AI Hub. In principle, it isn't exactly an obvious choice if all you really need is Home Assistant, but hear me out. The SwitchBot AI Hub runs containerized versions of Home Assistant and Frigate on a single device and offers OpenClaw support if you want to experiment with AI-powered control. This approach has some compromises, but it's astonishing how much works right out of the box. This palm-sized box has replaced three separate devices for me.

I replaced every cloud automation in my house with a local n8n workflow, and my smart home finally feels like mine

And none of my data leaves my house.

4
By  Anurag Singh

Home Assistant and Frigate in one compact box

The SwitchBot AI Hub solves my biggest smart home server problem

Home Assistant is the foundation of my smart home, and I use it to bring devices from different manufacturers into one interface and create automations that would otherwise require juggling multiple apps. Between Hue lights, Zigbee relays and smart switches, I wanted one place to manage everything, and Home Assistant gives me that flexibility.

Frigate handles the other half of my setup. I run a motley mix of RTSP-enabled cameras. Between Reolink and UniFi, Frigate is one of the few tools that can tie it all together, process camera streams, record footage, and even detect objects. In fact, you can even set it to identify people, vehicles, and other objects. That makes it easy to find relevant footage without scrubbing through hours of recordings.

The problem is that running object recognition and video processing is fairly processor-heavy, and my old Raspberry Pi was absolutely not up to the task. In fact, I had to remove Frigate from my Pi altogether because, during processing, it was prone to killing processes on my Home Assistant instance. That wasn't an option.

The SwitchBot AI Hub, on the other hand, is designed from the ground up to handle this workload. It includes support for both Frigate and Home Assistant Core. The hardware, too, includes an AI accelerator rated for 6 TOPS of performance. That's not class-leading by any stretch, but more than enough for the tasks the hub is meant to do. Put together, it is the appliance-style hub I was looking for.

While SwitchBot advertises the hub as a hub for its assortment of smart home devices, it also supports Home Assistant and Frigate equally well. In fact, you don't need to dabble in command-line tools or even a web interface to get either set up. The SwitchBot app includes one-tap installers for both, and you can update your Home Assistant instance directly from the mobile app.

Similarly, Frigate supports up to eight RTSP-compatible camera feeds. This lets you pull in cameras you might already have without buying SwitchBot-branded cameras. Coming from a Raspberry Pi that used to choke on two 4K cameras, this is a big upgrade.

Why I'd choose the SwitchBot AI Hub, despite its limitations

Very good, but not perfect

  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 
  • Credit:

  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 

After a few months with the hub, there's one major reason I'd choose the SwitchBot AI Hub over a Raspberry Pi:Frigate. Home Assistant alone isn't enough to justify the switch and investment because it is light enough to run on even an older Raspberry Pi if all you're doing is running a few basic automations and controlling lights, sensors, and switches.

That said, a fully integrated hub has some downsides. The biggest is the lack of control. For example, the SwitchBot Hub does not include Zigbee support, and you can't just plug in a Zigbee controller to the USB port. That's a big miss in my books, and if this is a use case for you, the AI Hub isn't going to work out. You can't directly integrate things like Hue lighting, Zigbee relays, or smart switches. In my case, I use a Hue integration, which works well enough for me, but might not for you.

Matter support isn't quite perfect either. The AI Hub can act as a Matter bridge for supported SwitchBot devices, exposing them to compatible smart home ecosystems. However, that isn’t the same as having Matter controller support built into the Home Assistant installation running on the device. With the SwitchBot AI Hub, you'll need to enable the SwitchBot integration and pull in your Matter integrations through it instead of connecting directly to Matter devices.

Depending on how in-depth you want to go with Home Assistant, you might run into one more limitation. The SwitchBot AI Hub runs Home Assistant Core in a container that doesn't include the Supervisor and app management offered by HAOS. So, your ability to install add-ons is going to be somewhat limited compared to a bare-metal Home Assistant install. That said, not everyone needs add-on support, and the Core experience works exceptionally well.

A simpler, but just as capable server for your smart home

The SwitchBot AI Hub makes a lot of sense to me as a Raspberry Pi alternative as long as you keep your expectations in check. It can handle reasonably complex automations and process multiple camera feeds in a compact and, frankly, visually appealing form factor. I'm not a big fan of giving AI tools unfettered access to my devices, but if you want to experiment, you can even install OpenClaw on the hub and use it to interact with your smart home via chat-based controls.

Yes, the Home Assistant instance isn't full-fledged HAOS, nor do you have unfettered access to the file system for installing additional ancillary software. But not everyone needs that. If your goal is to build a Home Assistant smart home as simply as possible, the SwitchBot AI Hub offers an easy way to do that.

item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I've written about Nvidia's Pascal lineup being their best one yet, and most gamers seem to agree. The iconic GTX 1080 Ti has a lot to do with that acclaim. The community fondly remembers it as the best GPU produced by Nvidia, possibly by any company. Its unmatched longevity and excellent performance per dollar made it a benchmark for flagship GPU performance.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Three and a half years later, Nvidia launched the RTX 3080, coincidentally at the same MSRP. It many not have been apparent at the time, but the 80-class Ampere card was destined to repeat what the GTX 1080 Ti did in the last decade. item.title: I made self-hosting harder than it needed to be by making this one mistake
item.itunes:title: I made self-hosting harder than it needed to be by making this one mistake
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Self-hosting gives me the freedom to run my own services, explore open-source tools, and keep more control over my data. What started as a fun hobby gradually grew into a bigger project than I expected. I was spending more time configuring my setup than enjoying the applications I hosted. Every weekend seemed to bring a new tweak, and my list of planned changes grew faster than I could work through it.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

The problem wasn't self-hosting itself. It was my habit of building for every possible scenario, including ones I never ran into. A straightforward setup rarely felt like enough when I could make something more flexible. Looking back, that one mistake made everything harder: I kept over-engineering things instead of focusing on what I needed.

I kept adding complexity that I didn't actually need

I optimized for problems I hadn't encountered yet

The more comfortable I became with self-hosting, the more I wanted to customize everything. I experimented with reverse proxies, custom Docker networks, environment variables, and extra configuration options, even when the default setup worked perfectly well.

For example, I could have reached a self-hosted application on my local network using its IP address and port. Instead, I was tempted to set up a reverse proxy, configure domain names, manage SSL certificates, and route traffic through additional services. That approach makes sense when you need remote access to multiple applications, but it's overkill for tools I only use at home.

I also found myself adding tools to improve other tools. If an application lacked a feature, I'd look for another service to fill the gap. Each addition felt like progress, but I wasn't always solving a problem I had.

Part of the appeal was that complexity looked like competence. Homelab forums and YouTube tours are full of elaborate stacks, and it's easy to treat them as the standard to aim for. But those setups are often built by people with different needs, more free time, or jobs that reward that kind of knowledge. Copying their architecture didn't give me their reasons for building it.

I thought self-hosting would save me money, but my years of experience proved otherwise

My self-hosted setup was supposed to cut costs, not become another expensive hobby.

5
By  Yash Patel

The hidden cost of over-engineering was maintenance

Every extra layer was one more thing to look after

The real cost showed up after the initial excitement wore off. Running the applications was only part of the job. I also had to keep everything updated, check that services were still working, and figure out what went wrong whenever something broke.

Even small changes could turn into time-consuming tasks. Before updating a container, I sometimes had to check its configuration to make sure nothing would break. When something went wrong, I had to dig through logs and check different components to find the cause. The more services depended on each other, the harder it became to pinpoint the problem.

Time made it worse. A clever tweak I made one weekend would be a mystery a few months later. When something failed, I often had to reverse-engineer my own decisions before I could fix anything, because I rarely documented why I had set things up that way.

My setup was taking far more time than it deserved, and the benefit of each extra layer rarely justified the upkeep. I needed a better way to decide what belonged in my homelab and what didn't.

My biggest self-hosting lesson was to stop over-engineering

Build for your needs, not possibilities

Now I judge my setup by how well it serves me, not by how advanced it looks. If an application runs reliably, I leave its configuration alone, even when another approach seems more interesting. Often, the smarter choice is to change nothing.

Before adding anything new, I run through a few quick questions. Does it solve a problem I have today? Will I use it regularly? Am I willing to keep it updated a year from now? If the answer to any of them is no, it stays on my list of things to try someday rather than becoming part of my homelab. I've also gone the other way and removed services I rarely opened, which made the rest of the setup easier to understand. For tools that never leave my home network, I went back to plain IP-and-port access and kept the reverse proxy only for the few services I need from outside.

That doesn't mean a complex homelab is a bad idea. Building one purely for the learning experience is a perfectly good reason. What matters is knowing whether the complexity serves a purpose or just creates work. For me, self-hosting is more enjoyable when it stays practical, and my tools run quietly in the background.

I hosted services for my family, and the real work started after setup

I started self-hosting to escape subscriptions, but I didn't expect to become the unpaid IT department for my family.

4
By  Yash Patel

The best homelab is the one that lets you get on with life

I still enjoy discovering new self-hosted tools and experimenting with my setup. But I no longer feel the need to install every interesting application or keep tweaking things just because I can. There's always something new to try, and that's part of the fun. I've simply learned to be more selective about what deserves a place in my homelab. After all, I started self-hosting to make my digital life easier, not to spend all my time managing it.

Now I judge my setup by how well it serves me, not by how advanced it looks. If an application runs reliably, I leave its configuration alone, even when another approach seems more interesting. Often, the smarter choice is to change nothing.

I started self-hosting to escape subscriptions, but I didn't expect to become the unpaid IT department for my family.

I still enjoy discovering new self-hosted tools and experimenting with my setup. But I no longer feel the need to install every interesting application or keep tweaking things just because I can. item.itunes:title: Your router keeps a list of every device that has ever connected, and some of them might not be yours
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
You might assume if your Wi-Fi password is secure and your guests only use the guest network, that your home network is an airtight fortress. However, log into your router's admin dashboard, dig into the DHCP client list or the ARP table, and you'll likely discover a graveyard of dozens or even hundreds of devices you don't recognize (spanning years of old phones, smart bulbs, IoT appliances, and strange MAC addresses).

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Routers don't just forget devices when they disconnect. They actually cache historical leases, leaving behind an audit trail that exposes who or what has historically tapped into your local perimeter. Your router's device history is the digital fingerprint of your home security footprint. Buried in those stale logs are forgotten legacy gadgets, under-managed smart home nodes, and potentially unauthorized devices lingering where they shouldn't be.

I reverse engineered my cheap managed switch's firmware

People asked why I trust this Switch, so here's part of my process of reverse engineering it.

By  Adam Conway

How do DHCP leases work?

It might not feel like a big deal

How do DHCP leases and ARP caches actually work? By understanding how routers store network ghost towns, you can actually understand the networking mechanics behind what your router tracks and why these lists persist. Routers assign IP addresses dynamically via DHCP, otherwise known as Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol. In order to prevent IP collisions, routers maintain a lease table that remembers MAC addresses, hostnames, and IP bindings after a device leaves the physical premises.

This leads to a whole lot of legacy clutter. Consumer router firmware rarely garbage collects old entries aggressively. Sometimes some devices may disappear, but there's never a full purge of all of your old IP addresses. Every time a friend visited with their phone (even if it was five years ago) or an old smart TV connected once during setup, its MAC address remains etched into the router's non-volatile memory or active state tables.

Clogged tables can be a security risk

Don't let stray devices stay connected

You might wonder what these tables are for and why it's important to understand and access them. In reality, auditing them might give you some insight into a lot of these mysterious devices lurking in your router table.

For the most part, many are harmless phantoms, like old smartphones you got rid of, IoT gadgets you returned, or smart light bulbs that ping the network once before being factory reset. These, for the most part, are devices you don't have to worry about.

On top of this, you'll have the Mac randomization blow with modern mobile OS features like iOS and Android generating dozens of pseudo-unique device names that clog up your DHCP tables. This might look like your device has been invaded by a dozen unknown gadgets, when in reality it is the same device generating its own IP address over and over again.

However, the real security risks are unsecured neighbors reaching for a weak signal, rogue IoT devices phoning home without your knowledge, or legacy hardware left with default credentials that can serve as backdoors for hackers to enter your home and network.

Pull off a network audit now

Ensure your network is secure

If you want to sort through all these devices, purge your router logs, and secure your airspace, the first step is an audit.

Start by accessing your router's advanced status pages. Bypass the simplified mobile app and log into your router's web interface to find the DHCP clients, DHCP leases, or ARP table. If you're struggling, contact your ISP to find out how to obtain this information.

Once you've done this, you should export and clean house. Clear out any stale, expired leases and factory reset ghosts that haven't been on the network in months. You can cross-reference active clients too by matching every currently connected device against your physical inventory. Rename any ambiguous hostnames so you instantly recognize every device on your subnet.

Lastly, it's time to lock down access control. You can implement MAC address filtering, assign static IPs to trusted hardware, and segregate unverified IoT gadgets onto an isolated guest or IoT VLAN.

When you do this, note that you might have to decipher some OUI codes, also known as organizationally unique identifier codes. Often, you can look up the first six digits of a mysterious MAC address, which might help you identify the manufacturer. This will give you a little bit more information than relying on the confusing device hostnames alone.

You will still likely have to deal with constant MAC rotation. Balancing your mobile privacy settings against home network management can be frustrating because mobile phones shuffle their MAC addresses every time they reconnect to Wi-Fi. Be sure to double-check your phone settings if this is something that's clogging your table.

Don't ignore your logs

They might cause problems later down the line

Your router remembers everything that has ever touched your network. Ignoring those logs means leaving your digital perimeter open to invisible clutter and lingering security liabilities. Stop treating your router as a set-and-forget-it black box. Instead, log into your dashboard tonight, inspect your device lists, and clean house.

item.title: Jellyfin supports 7 hardware transcoding methods — here's which one your server can use
item.itunes:title: Jellyfin supports 7 hardware transcoding methods — here's which one your server can use
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Jellyfin is pretty good at playing your media without much fuss, but things get considerably more complicated when it has to transcode a video on the fly. It can prove to be a ton of work for your humble home server to decode a 4K HDR movie, convert its audio, burn subtitles into the picture, and encode everything into a format your client can actually play.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Thankfully, Jellyfin supports several hardware acceleration methods that can take some of that workload off the processor. The catch, of course, is that these methods aren't interchangeable. As such, it's the hardware sitting inside your server that determines which options are available to you. Understanding these differences is particularly useful when you're building a media server on a budget or trying to squeeze more life out of hardware you already own.

I built a 4K Jellyfin server with Intel Quick Sync for under $200, and it's enough to replace my old GPU setup

Intel's Quick Sync is a game-changer for media transcoding tasks

4
By  Ayush Pande

Nvidia GPUs are excellent transcoding workhorses with NVDEC/NVENC

Your GeForce GPU has a job beyond rendering games

NVIDIA splits its hardware video acceleration into two components: NVDEC handles video decoding, while NVENC handles encoding. Jellyfin can use both to transcode media without forcing your CPU to do all the heavy lifting. If you're planning on repurposing an older GeForce card, that's potentially a lot of transcoding muscle sitting around waiting for something useful to do.

However, keep in mind that while Nvidia did introduce NVENC encoders starting with the GeForce Kepler 600 series, those cards would be terrible for a modern Jellyfin server. First-gen NVENC had very low framerates, no 10-bit color support, and only supported H.264 and MPEG-2. Most modern media libraries use H.265 or AV1 to save space today.

My "obsolete" RTX 2070 Super still games, streams, and sharpens my video, and it's only getting started

There's no silicon worth wasting

By  Abhinav Raj

The minimum recommendation for an Nvidia GPU with NVENC support would be either a GTX 1650 Super or a GTX 1660 with Turing architecture, since these cards support 6th-gen NVENC encoding with excellent H.264/H.265 visual quality and plenty of power for multiple (and simultaneous) 4K HDR transcodes.

Best of all, your GPU doesn't need a monitor connected to it. A headless Jellyfin server can use NVENC and NVDEC just fine, making that spare graphics card considerably more useful than its gaming benchmarks suggest.

MSI Ventus 2X GeForce RTX 3060 12GB
$600 at Newegg See at Amazon

Intel Quick Sync Video is a reliable home server companion

Intel's integrated graphics can do more than display your desktop

Intel Quick Sync Video uses dedicated media-processing hardware in supported Intel GPUs to accelerate video decoding and encoding. That means your processor doesn't have to shoulder the entire transcoding workload, which is particularly useful when you're running Jellyfin on a modest home server.

Quick Sync Video works on both Windows and Linux, but the support depends entirely on your Intel GPU generation, drivers, and codecs. The primary candidates, of course, are Intel Core CPUs that ship with integrated graphics (iGPUs) and Intel's ARC GPUs. Just remember that an Intel processor doesn't automatically guarantee QSV support; some models lack integrated graphics entirely.

QSV is understandably appealing to many home server enthusiasts, since it offers hardware-accelerated transcoding without requiring a separate graphics card. You can build a relatively inexpensive, power-efficient Jellyfin server that handles demanding video workloads without turning your electricity bill into another monthly subscription.

Intel Quick Sync is the reason I will never buy another Nvidia card for my Jellyfin server

Quick Sync is just that effective for self-hosted media server setups

1
By  Ayush Pande

AMD's Advanced Media Framework (AMF) is Windows-exclusive

Radeon GPUs can transcode your media, too

AMD's Advanced Media Framework (AMF) lets Jellyfin access the dedicated video-processing capabilities of supported Radeon GPUs. Much like NVIDIA's NVENC and NVDEC, it enables hardware-accelerated video encoding and decoding, freeing your CPU to handle other server duties instead of working overtime on every transcoded stream.

However, Jellyfin's AMF implementation is designed only for Windows. If you've got an AMD GPU and are running Linux, you should look at VA-API instead, which provides a different route to hardware acceleration. Compatibility also depends on your specific Radeon GPU, its drivers, and the codecs involved, so don't assume that every feature will work across every generation.

Vintage AMD Radeon GPUs are getting a second life with AI-optimized Linux drivers

Keeping older AMD GPUs alive.

2
By  Rich Edmonds

Among older Radeon GPUs, the RX 500 series is a good starting point, since it would have support for H.264 as well as HEVC (H.265) decoding, and encoding capabilities as well. For newer media, a Radeon RX 6000 series would be the card to get, since RDNA 2 architecture is when AV1 decoding came to AMD GPUs.

If you plan on using an AMD card for Jellyfin transcoding, make sure you check Jellyfin's compatibility documentation before building your server around any particular Radeon model.

VA-API gives Linux another way to accelerate transcoding

Linux has its own way of talking to your GPU

VA-API (Video Acceleration API) is a Linux-only route to hardware video acceleration, used by Intel and AMD graphics. Instead of being tied to any particular manufacturer’s proprietary framework, VA-API gives software such as Jellyfin a common interface for accessing supported video-decoding and encoding hardware in practice.

Now, Jellyfin still recommends Quick Sync Video on Intel systems, especially on mainstream hardware. It's mostly on AMD GPUs running Linux that VA-API is especially useful, since it supports full acceleration on Polaris-based Radeon RX 400/500 cards and newer.

Depending on the GPU, driver, and codec, that can include decoding, encoding, scaling, and other pipeline stages. It's important to know that VA-API is not an option on Windows, and Linux support still depends on compatible drivers and Jellyfin’s recommended jellyfin-ffmpeg build.

Hardware transcoding matters less than you think if you pick the right clients

It all comes down to what's receiving the stream

21
By  Rich Edmonds

Apple VideoToolbox puts your Mac's media hardware to work

Your Mac's media engine can pull its weight

Apple VideoToolbox is Jellyfin's hardware acceleration method for macOS, giving the server access to the dedicated media engines built into supported Apple hardware. Instead of making your CPU sweat through every transcoding job, VideoToolbox offloads compatible video decoding and encoding to specialized hardware, helping keep power consumption and processor utilization under control.

You don't need a discrete graphics card or a particularly beefy Mac to benefit from this, either. Apple Silicon, including the M1 chip and newer Macs, support hardware acceleration for formats like H.264 and HEVC. Codec support still varies, though, and AV1 remains a pretty notable limitation in Jellyfin's current macOS transcoding pipeline.

Regardless, it's pretty common for users to repurpose old Mac mini units as a media server, and VideoToolbox makes them pretty good candidates. However, if you're the kind of power user who installs Linux on their Mac, this won't work, since VideoToolbox is a macOS-only option.

Jellyfin does hardware transcoding for free, and Plex wants $250 to match it

Jellyfin gives you free hardware transcoding, while Plex charges $250 for the same capability. The value gap keeps growing.

50
By  Jeff Butts

Even ARM media servers are viable with Rockchip RKMPP

Your next media server might not even need an x86 chip

Rockchip's Media Process Platform (RKMPP) lets Jellyfin tap into the dedicated video-processing hardware found in compatible ARM-based systems. Unlike the Raspberry Pi's increasingly limited transcoding support, RKMPP offers a genuinely capable solution for supported Rockchip chips, including the RK3588 and RK3588S.

If you're determined to build a compact, power-efficient server instead of repurposing an old PC that guzzles electricity, this is a pretty appealing alternative.

RKMPP is not supported on Windows, but is supported on Linux. It also requires Jellyfin 10.9 or newer. On compatible hardware, it enables accelerated decoding, encoding, scaling, pixel-format conversions, and subtitle burn-in through dedicated processing components.

Jellyfin specifically recommends the RK3588 and RK3588S; older Rockchip chips have more limited capabilities. Check compatibility before buying.

Everytime I set up a new Jellyfin server, these are the plugins I install first

These add-ons bring Jellyfin up to par with its premium, paid rivals

3
By  Samarveer Singh

Raspberry Pi's hardware acceleration is a bit of a mess

Your tiny home server has some pretty big limitations

Raspberry Pi boards seem perfect for a low-power Jellyfin server, until you ask them to transcode video. Even though earlier models offered hardware acceleration through OpenMAX, Jellyfin ended up dropping that support in version 10.8. It was replaced with V4L2, the official Linux kernel API, but it never matured into a reliable, fully supported option, and has since been deprecated.

That doesn't make a Raspberry Pi useless for Jellyfin, though. Direct play works perfectly well when your client supports the original media's codecs, letting the Pi serve files without transcoding them. However, it's best to temper your expectations on this front, though — don't go assuming it will effortlessly convert a 4K HDR movie for an incompatible device.

The Pi 5 is particularly disappointing here: it lacks dedicated hardware video encoders. Use one for lightweight media serving, but consider an Intel mini PC if transcoding is a priority.

The Raspberry Pi Zero 2W is a small SBC, but Jellyfin tends to work surprisingly better than you anticipate.

By  Abhishek Kumar Mishra

Jellyfin gives you more ways to transcode than you might think

I've come to love and appreciate how little Jellyfin demands of you in the way of software before it can get you started on your self-hosting journey. You could be repurposing an old office PC, trying to find another use of an old GPU collecting dust in the drawer, or even experimenting with ARM-based single-board computers, but there's a good chance that your Jellyfin setup will work on that hardware.

Of course, the trick is to know exactly which route your hardware supports so you can stay abreast of your server. Regardless, it's nothing short of impressive that Jellyfin doesn't ask you to lock yourself into buying a specific GPU or build a fully new machine just to serve your media. With the right combination of hardware, drivers, and configuration, even an unlikely little home server can punch well above its weight.

Jellyfin is one of the best Plex alternatives you can get, and that's thanks to its open-source nature and powerful set of features. There are apps for basically every platform and it's completely free to run your very own server.
